messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame, a 59-year-old professor of African descent, still remembers the late summer afternoon three years ago when his younger brother, Kofi, drowned during a flash flood in a nearby ravine. Kwame had been the one to find him after the water receded, the smell of wet earth and decay lingering in the air. He had tried to pull Kofi out, but his brother was already gone. That single image—the still, muddy water, the silence—lodged itself somewhere inside him.

In the months that followed, Kwame noticed that everyday sights began to carry a charge he could not control. A garden hose left running on campus, a student’s water bottle spilling across a desk, the sudden smell of damp concrete after a rain shower—each one made his chest tighten before his mind could catch up. His body would react to danger before he had even had time to think: his heart would hammer, his breath would catch, and he would feel a wave of fear or horror that seemed to come from nowhere. He knew he was not in danger, but the feelings were overwhelming.

Kwame, who had always prided himself on his composure in the lecture hall, found himself unable to relax even when he knew he was in a safe place. The campus pool, which he had once walked past without a second thought, became a place he avoided entirely. He began taking longer routes to his office to stay away from any fountain or drainage grate. The smell of dampness after the janitor mopped the hallway would send him into a spiral of anger and shame that lasted hours. He had come to believe that his own body was betraying him, that the world was full of hidden reminders he could not outrun.

The more hypervigilant he became, the more triggers he seemed to encounter. Stress, in particular, amplified the loop. During grading season or faculty meetings, he would notice the faintest hint of humidity in the air and immediately be flooded with the memory of that afternoon. His body would react before his mind—a cold sweat, a tensing of his shoulders—and then the negative emotions would surge: guilt for not having saved Kofi, horror at the memory, anger at his own powerlessness. He became certain that he could not predict when the next trigger would ambush him, so he tried to anticipate every possible cue. But that only made him more sensitive.

At work, he started cancelling office hours that coincided with the building’s sprinkler schedule. He asked for a reassignment to a windowless classroom to avoid the view of a small pond behind the science building. His colleagues noticed he was jumpy and withdrawn, and his teaching evaluations slipped as students sensed his distraction. He felt isolated, but he could not bring himself to explain why the sight of even a puddle could paralyse him.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was a departmental meeting held in a conference room adjacent to the campus aquarium. He had walked in, caught the faint briny smell, and immediately experienced a dissociative surge—he felt as if he were back in the ravine, helpless. He had to excuse himself to the restroom, where he wept silently. That night, he admitted to himself that he could no longer manage the loop alone. He was terrified that his body would never stop reacting, that he would always be caught in the moment before thought, and that the world would always feel dangerous. But he also hoped that somewhere, a professional could help him find a way to break the cycle—to let water be just water again, and to let Kofi rest.
